correctness.rationale: Projection gives a Minkowski sum of the projected base and a segment of length h√(1−z²), with z=U_3. On lines parallel to the segment the chord lengths increase by its length; integration gives the planar area increment as length times transverse width, also for a degenerate base projection at z=0. The base determinant factor is |z| and the transverse direction is horizontal and perpendicular to the azimuth. The poles give B_h=A. Thus with Z=|U_3| uniform on [0,1], B_h=AZ+h√(1−Z²)W where W is independent of Z and has the base's uniform-direction width law. Conditional variance contributes exactly (2/3)h²(ν−μ²); the variance of the conditional mean contributes A²/12−Aμqh+μ²gh², using the integrals π/4 for √(1−Z²) and 1/3 for Z√(1−Z²). Cauchy's planar perimeter formula gives μ=per(Q)/π. Both q and g are strictly positive (g is itself a variance), so completing the square gives the unique positive optimizer, the minimum, and the increasing excess. By continuity, zero width variance is equivalent to constant width in every direction. At equality t=q/(2g)>1, and the graph of z+t√(1−z²) has endpoints t and 1 and maximum √(1+t²) at z=1/√(1+t²). The larger quadratic root is the endpoint of the descending-branch sublevel interval, and for y≥t the smaller root adds the ascending-branch sublevel length; both formulas agree at y=t and are valid at 1 and at the maximum. This also gives strictly positive variance. The decimal checks give t≈1.191691057107415, C_*≈0.012587701907808, and disk h_*/R≈1.871903935178654.
residual_risks: Packaged code inspected, not executed. Its midpoint quadrature uses the brightness formula rather than proving it, and its finite checks do not test the full-law CDF.

Independent geometric spot-check replay: project the six vertices of the prism over (0,0),(3,0),(1,2) at height h=0.8, z=0.23 and azimuth φ=1.4. Planar coordinates are (−x sin φ+y cos φ, z(x cos φ+y sin φ)−√(1−z²) times the vertical coordinate). Convex hull and shoelace give area 2.991673061727096, in agreement with the predicted formula; the chord argument establishes the universal result.
The limitations phrase about full laws should be read as excluding general bases, not the stated constant-width equality law.

originality.rationale: Supported distinct content is the optimum and sharp rigidity profile under fixed base-area normalization, together with the full normalized equality-law shared by all planar constant-width bases. The shadow decomposition is classical; cube and rectangular-prism moments and circular-cylinder brightness are not new. A later indexed right-prism result reproduces the arbitrary-base moment calculation and has constant-width optimal bases for a different objective. That substantial overlap is credited without equating the optimized objectives or claiming historical priority from the search.
residual_risks: Small's JSTOR article was not available in full; other older brightness or caliper formulations may contain further overlap. This bounded comparison does not establish priority.
The later mean-normalized result's exact common moment polynomial limits the independent scope of the calculation; the two normalizations must remain explicit.

value.rationale: Optimizing height at fixed base-area scale gives a complete, geometrically interpretable comparison for arbitrary bases: a single angular width statistic quantifies the entire increase of optimal variance over a sharp bound and excludes every nonconstant-width base. The optimizers include nondisk and nonsmooth examples and share a full normalized law, not just a moment. This resolves a natural sharp extremal question after the classical projection decomposition rather than reporting another special-body moment.
residual_risks: The deficit measures spread of widths, not distance to a particular disk or a quantitative Hausdorff stability statement. It is not an optimized coefficient of variation or a law for general oblique prisms.
